claim: Breakdown of neuromuscular junctions (NMJs) is an early pathological hallmark of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).
source: Breakdown of neuromuscular junctions (NMJs) is an early pathological hallmark of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) that blocks neuromuscular transmission, leading to muscle weakness, paralysis and, ultimately, premature death.
evidence: This is a well-established finding in ALS research, supported by scientific consensus.

claim: Currently, no therapies exist that can prevent progressive motor neuron degeneration, muscle denervation, or paralysis in ALS.
source: Currently, no therapies exist that can prevent progressive motor neuron degeneration, muscle denervation, or paralysis in ALS.
evidence: This represents the current state of ALS treatment based on established medical knowledge.

claim: An optogenetic neural replacement strategy can effectively restore innervation of severely affected skeletal muscles in the aggressive SOD1G93A mouse model of ALS.
source: Here, we report important advances in the development of an optogenetic, neural replacement strategy that can effectively restore innervation of severely affected skeletal muscles in the aggressive SOD1G93A mouse model of ALS, thus providing an interface to selectively control the function of targeted muscles using optical stimulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript, including histological and physiological analyses.

claim: H57-597 mAb treatment confers complete survival of allogeneic replacement motor neurons.
source: We also identify a specific approach to confer complete survival of allogeneic replacement motor neurons.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing graft survival in all treated animals.

claim: An optical stimulation training paradigm can prevent atrophy of reinnervated muscle fibers.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrate that an optical stimulation training paradigm can prevent atrophy of reinnervated muscle fibers and results in a tenfold increase in optically evoked contractile force.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the dCALMS analysis showing muscle fiber cross-sectional areas.

claim: Optical stimulation training results in a tenfold increase in optically evoked contractile force.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrate that an optical stimulation training paradigm can prevent atrophy of reinnervated muscle fibers and results in a tenfold increase in optically evoked contractile force.
evidence: This is supported by isometric muscle tension physiology data comparing trained and untrained mice.

claim: One of the earliest characteristic pathological features of ALS involves 'die-back' of motor axon terminals.
source: However, one of the earliest characteristic pathological features of ALS involves 'die-back' of motor axon terminals (Fischer et al., 2004) and breakdown of neuromuscular junctions (NMJs), the specialized synapses between motor axon terminals and muscle fibres.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Fischer et al., 2004.

claim: The median survival time in ALS, from initial onset of symptoms to death, is 20–48 months.
source: The median survival time in ALS, from initial onset of symptoms to death, typically as a result of respiratory complications, is only 20–48 months (Chiò et al., 2009) and ALS has an estimated global mortality of 30,000 patients per year (Mathis et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chiò et al., 2009.

claim: ALS has an estimated global mortality of 30,000 patients per year.
source: The median survival time in ALS, from initial onset of symptoms to death, typically as a result of respiratory complications, is only 20–48 months (Chiò et al., 2009) and ALS has an estimated global mortality of 30,000 patients per year (Mathis et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mathis et al., 2019.

claim: Between 5% and 10% of total ALS cases are familial (fALS).
source: ALS is typically classified into either familial (fALS) or sporadic (sALS) forms of the disease, based on whether or not patients have an identified family history of the disease; between 5% and 10% of total ALS cases fall into the former category, fALS, with the remaining 90–95% consisting of sALS cases (Mathis et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mathis et al., 2019.

claim: Over 20 monogenic mutations that cause ALS have been identified.
source: To date, over 20 monogenic mutations that cause ALS have been identified; however, these still only account for 45% of fALS cases and only 7% of sALS cases (Mejzini et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mejzini et al., 2019.

claim: Identified monogenic mutations account for 45% of fALS cases and only 7% of sALS cases.
source: To date, over 20 monogenic mutations that cause ALS have been identified; however, these still only account for 45% of fALS cases and only 7% of sALS cases (Mejzini et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mejzini et al., 2019.

claim: There are currently no effective treatments capable of arresting the progressive paralysis that occurs in ALS.
source: Given the disparate causes and complex disease mechanisms, development of an effective therapy has proven extremely challenging and there are currently no effective treatments capable of arresting the progressive paralysis that occurs in ALS (Brown and Al-Chalabi, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Brown and Al-Chalabi, 2017.

claim: Antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) have shown early promise in clinical trials for ALS.
source: Even emergent gene therapy approaches, such as antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) that have shown early promise in clinical trials (Miller et al., 2013), are unlikely to benefit the majority of patients with sporadic ALS and will not replace degenerated motor neurons or restore motor function once it has been lost.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Miller et al., 2013.

claim: ASOs are unlikely to benefit the majority of patients with sporadic ALS.
source: Even emergent gene therapy approaches, such as antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) that have shown early promise in clinical trials (Miller et al., 2013), are unlikely to benefit the majority of patients with sporadic ALS and will not replace degenerated motor neurons or restore motor function once it has been lost.
evidence: This is based on inference from the fact that ASOs target specific genetic mutations which are not present in most sporadic ALS cases.

claim: Intraspinal engraftment of foetally derived neural stem cells (NSCs) has been used to slow motor neuron degeneration in ALS.
source: Similarly, efforts to develop cell therapy approaches for ALS have, so far, primarily been aimed at slowing the degeneration of motor neurons in the spinal cord by providing neurotrophic factor (NTF) support through intraspinal engraftment of foetally derived neural stem cells (NSCs; Feldman et al., 2014; Goutman et al., 2018) or intrathecal delivery of autologous mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) that are modified to overexpress NTFs (Cudkowicz et al., 2022; Berry et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Feldman et al., 2014 and Goutman et al., 2018.

claim: Clinical trials in ALS patients have shown only a modest therapeutic effect of intraspinal NSC grafts.
source: Whilst these approaches were shown to significantly slow disease progression in transgenic animal models of ALS (Xu et al., 2006; Yan et al., 2006), clinical trials in ALS patients have shown only a modest therapeutic effect in the case of intraspinal NSC grafts (Glass et al., 2012) and no overall benefit of intrathecal MSC delivery (Cudkowicz et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Glass et al., 2012.

claim: Intrathecal MSC delivery showed no overall benefit in ALS clinical trials.
source: Whilst these approaches were shown to significantly slow disease progression in transgenic animal models of ALS (Xu et al., 2006; Yan et al., 2006), clinical trials in ALS patients have shown only a modest therapeutic effect in the case of intraspinal NSC grafts (Glass et al., 2012) and no overall benefit of intrathecal MSC delivery (Cudkowicz et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cudkowicz et al., 2022.

claim: ALS patients can tolerate a 6-month period of immunosuppression.
source: Importantly, this pioneering approach provides a precedent for implementation of an allogeneic stem cell-based therapy and also shows that ALS patients can tolerate a 6-month period of immunosuppression (Mazzini et al., 2015), which appears to be sufficient to confer long-term survival of engrafted cells (Tadesse et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mazzini et al., 2015.

claim: A 6-month period of immunosuppression appears to be sufficient to confer long-term survival of engrafted cells.
source: Importantly, this pioneering approach provides a precedent for implementation of an allogeneic stem cell-based therapy and also shows that ALS patients can tolerate a 6-month period of immunosuppression (Mazzini et al., 2015), which appears to be sufficient to confer long-term survival of engrafted cells (Tadesse et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tadesse et al., 2014.

claim: Optogenetically modified replacement motor neurons can be engrafted into distal branches of peripheral nerves to restore control of muscle contraction.
source: We have previously demonstrated a novel proof-of-concept strategy to overcome muscle denervation and restore control of muscle contraction in a nerve injury model of muscle paralysis that could have major therapeutic value for restoring function of any targeted muscle or group of muscles in ALS patients (Bryson et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bryson et al., 2014.

claim: Engrafted motor neurons can project axons from the graft site to target muscles where they form de novo NMJs.
source: Our results showed that the engrafted motor neurons were able to project axons from the graft site to the target muscles where they formed de novo NMJs.
evidence: This claim is supported by previous work cited (Bryson et al., 2014) and confirmed by data in the current manuscript.

claim: Expression of ChR2 in engrafted motor neurons confers the ability to selectively activate these neurons using optical stimulation.
source: Expression of the blue-light sensitive channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2) protein (Nagel et al., 2003) in the engrafted motor neurons conferred the ability to selectively activate these engrafted neurons and thereby control the contractile function of the target muscle using acute optical stimulation (Bryson et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Nagel et al., 2003 and Bryson et al., 2014.

claim: A prototype 64-channel stimulation and recording device has been developed capable of controlling multiple independent intraneural graft sites.
source: Importantly, we have recently developed a prototype 64-channel stimulation and recording device capable of controlling multiple independent intraneural graft sites that could be used to elicit coordinated function of large numbers of muscles, in order to restore useful motor functions (Liu et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2022.

claim: Optical nerve stimulation (ONS) can recruit motor units in correct physiological order.
source: the ability to recruit motor units in correct physiological order using optical nerve stimulation (ONS; Llewellyn et al., 2010) avoids the problem of rapid muscle fatigue associated with ENS and incorrect, non-physiological motor unit recruitment.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Llewellyn et al., 2010.

claim: Electrical nerve stimulation (ENS) applied to the phrenic nerve accelerated diaphragm muscle denervation in ALS patients.
source: More importantly, it has recently been shown that ENS, applied to the phrenic nerve to assist respiratory function in two separate clinical trials in ALS patients (McDermott et al., 2016; Gonzalez-Bermejo et al., 2016), accelerated diaphragm muscle denervation, which likely contributed to a significant reduction in patient life-span (Guimarães-Costa et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to McDermott et al., 2016, Gonzalez-Bermejo et al., 2016, and Guimarães-Costa et al., 2019.

claim: In the absence of immunosuppression, the survival rate of ChR2+ motor neuron grafts at 35 d post engraftment was extremely low (<5%) in SOD1G93A mice.
source: In the absence of any immunosuppression, the survival rate of ChR2+ motor neuron grafts at 35 d post engraftment was extremely low (<5%) in SOD1G93A mice.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations from the study.

claim: In rare cases where engrafted ChR2+ motor neurons survived without immunosuppression, robust intramuscular axon growth and partial reinnervation of NMJs was observed.
source: However, in the rare cases where the engrafted ChR2+ motor neurons did survive, we observed robust intramuscular axon growth and partial reinnervation of NMJs, even at very late-stage disease (Figure 1A–C and Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 1A-C and Video 1.

claim: Acute optical stimulation of engrafted ChR2+ motor neurons induced tetanic contraction of the target muscle in SOD1G93A mice, although these were weak in magnitude.
source: Furthermore, acute optical stimulation of the engrafted ChR2+ motor neurons was able to induce tetanic contraction of the target muscle in these SOD1G93A mice (Figure 1D), although these were weak in magnitude.
evidence: This is supported by physiological data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Poor long-term survival of engrafted ChR2+ motor neurons was likely due to host-vs-graft rejection rather than disease-related toxicity.
source: It is therefore likely that the poor long-term survival was due to host-vs-graft rejection of the engrafted cells, rather than disease-related toxicity.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that grafts survived up to 14 days and that immunosuppression enabled long-term survival.

claim: FK506 enabled robust ChR2+ motor neuron allograft survival at the graft site in all animals examined.
source: Although FK506 did enable robust ChR2+ motor neuron allograft survival, at the graft site, in all animals examined (Appendix 1—table 2), we identified three major problems with this immunosuppressant agent.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations from the study.

claim: FK506 completely prevented muscle fibre reinnervation by engrafted motor neurons.
source: Firstly, although the engrafted motor neurons were able to survive and project axons along peripheral nerve branches and within the targeted lower hindlimb muscles (Figure 2A), FK506 completely prevented muscle fibre reinnervation, evidenced by lack of response to acute ONS (data not shown) and complete absence of ChR2+/YFP+ NMJs (Figure 2B) in both SOD1G93A (n=8) and nerve-ligated wild-type mice (n=4).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 2B and lack of physiological response.

claim: FK506 treatment led to intraneural tumour formation in most mice.
source: Secondly, exuberant growth of carry-over pluripotent stem cells led to intraneural tumour formation in most mice (Figure 2C and Appendix 1—table 2), which resulted in overt hindlimb motor deficits (Figure 2D and Video 2).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 2C and behavioral observations in Figure 2D and Video 2.

claim: FK506 prevented body mass increase and/or induced body mass decline in 44.4% of SOD1G93A mice.
source: Thirdly, in partial agreement with previous reports in rats (Aydin et al., 2004), FK506 prevented body mass increase and/or induced body mass decline in a subset (44.4%; n=8/18) of SOD1G93A mice (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A); this effect was less evident in wild-type mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by longitudinal body mass data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: FK506 caused a significant loss of axons in the tibial nerve and common peroneal nerve in wild-type and SOD1G93A mice.
source: Indeed, examination of the cross-sectional area distribution of total (i.e. sensory and motor) and motor neuron axons in branches of the sciatic nerve in FK506-treated SOD1G93A and WT mice (Figure 3A) revealed a significant loss of axons that affected most axonal calibres in the tibial nerve in wild-type and SOD1G93A mice (Figure 3B and C). A more pronounced loss of total and motor axons, spanning medium to large sized axonal calibres, was observed in the common peroneal nerve branch (Figure 3D and E), which indicates that FK506 can not only exacerbate ongoing motor axon loss in SOD1G93A mice but can also induce motor axon loss even in wild-type mice.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative axon analysis data shown in Figure 3.

claim: H57-597 mAb treatment does not significantly alter total or motor axon size distribution or total axon counts compared to untreated SOD1G93A mice.
source: Importantly, these neuropathy-like effects appear to be specific to FK-506, since an alternative immunosuppressant, H57-597 mAb (discussed in detail below), did not significantly alter total or motor axon size distribution or total axon counts (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), compared to untreated SOD1G93A mice.
evidence: This is supported by axon analysis data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: FK506 is known to suppress myoblast proliferation and differentiation.
source: Since FK506 is known to suppress myoblast proliferation and differentiation (Hong et al., 2002) and can cause rare cases of myopathy in humans (Breil and Chariot, 1999), it is also possible that the FK506-dependent prevention of muscle reinnervation by engrafted ChR2+ motor neurons is due to a muscle specific effect.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hong et al., 2002 and Breil and Chariot, 1999.

claim: H57-597 mAb has been shown to effectively promote long-term heart allograft survival in mice.
source: Therefore, we investigated the T-cell receptor-β (TCR-β) targeting monoclonal antibody, mAb H57-597, which has previously been shown to effectively promote long-term heart allograft survival in mice (Miyahara et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Miyahara et al., 2012.

claim: Mitomycin-C (MMC) pre-treatment of differentiated ChR2+ motor neurons eliminates tumorigenic cells.
source: In addition, since our findings indicated that immunosuppression results in a greater risk of tumour formation from carry-over pluripotent stem cells, differentiated ChR2+ motor neurons were also pre-treated with mitomycin-C (MMC; 2 μg/ml for 2 hr) prior to engraftment, to eliminate tumorigenic cells (Magown et al., 2016), to further enhance the translational potential.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Magown et al., 2016.

claim: Engrafted ChR2+ motor neurons were present in all recipient SOD1G93A mice treated with H57-597 mAb (n>84 to date).
source: Histological analysis confirmed that in mAb H57-597 treated animals, engrafted ChR2+ motor neurons were present in all recipient SOD1G93A mice (n>84 to date).
evidence: This is based on histological analysis of all treated animals.

claim: There was significant axonal projection within intramuscular nerve branches and robust reinnervation of muscle fibres in H57-597 treated SOD1G93A mice.
source: Importantly, there was significant axonal projection within intramuscular nerve branches and robust reinnervation of muscle fibres in the targeted TS muscle (Figure 4A, B; Videos 3 and 4).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 4A, B and Videos 3 and 4.

claim: Some de novo NMJs in SOD1G93A mice exhibited signs of immaturity, including poly-innervation.
source: As we previously reported in a wild-type mouse nerve ligation model Bryson et al., 2014, some de novo NMJs in SOD1G93A mice exhibited signs of immaturity, including poly-innervation (Figure 4C), as well as collateral and terminal sprouting of motor axons (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 4C and 4D.

claim: Only 10.5% of endplates are innervated by engrafted ChR2+ motor neurons.
source: Since the peripherally-engrafted reinnervating motor neurons are inactive during the post-engraftment period and progressive muscle atrophy is ongoing, only 10.5% of endplates are innervated by engrafted ChR2+ motor neurons (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of endplate innervation shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Acute in vivo ONS of engrafted ChR2+ motor neurons induced positive contractile responses in all late-stage SOD1G93A mice tested.
source: Importantly, these reinnervated endplates are functional, since acute in vivo ONS of the engrafted ChR2+ motor neurons in the exposed sciatic nerve of late-stage disease SOD1G93A mice at 133±7.2 days of age (37.7±5.1 days post-engraftment; n=12), induced positive contractile responses in all animals, although the amplitude of the maximal contractile force was still weak (0.8±0.2 g; n=11).
evidence: This is based on isometric muscle tension physiology data from all tested animals.

claim: Motor neuron subtype identity did not significantly affect amplitude of the muscle response to acute optical stimulation.
source: This physiological analysis revealed that the motor neuron subtype identity did not significantly affect amplitude of the muscle response to acute optical stimulation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and Appendix 1—table 3) and that the maximum contractile force elicited by ONS remained extremely weak compared to supra-maximal ENS (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and Appendix 1—table 3).
evidence: This is supported by physiological data comparing fast-firing and slow-firing motor neurons shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Spinal motor circuit development is an activity-dependent process.
source: Spinal motor circuit development (Milner and Landmesser, 1999; Li et al., 2005) and NMJ formation/maintenance (Sanes and Lichtman, 1999) are known to be activity-dependent processes, thus, without regular stimulation, although peripherally engrafted ChR2+ motor neurons may survive, they are unlikely to form mature NMJs and will therefore have little effect on declining muscle function and atrophy in SOD1G93A mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Milner and Landmesser, 1999 and Li et al., 2005.

claim: NMJ formation/maintenance is an activity-dependent process.
source: Spinal motor circuit development (Milner and Landmesser, 1999; Li et al., 2005) and NMJ formation/maintenance (Sanes and Lichtman, 1999) are known to be activity-dependent processes, thus, without regular stimulation, although peripherally engrafted ChR2+ motor neurons may survive, they are unlikely to form mature NMJs and will therefore have little effect on declining muscle function and atrophy in SOD1G93A mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sanes and Lichtman, 1999.

claim: Daily optical stimulation training (OST) resulted in a 9.4-fold increase in maximal tetanic force compared to untrained SOD1G93A mice.
source: In confirmation of our hypothesis, there was a highly significant, 9.4-fold, increase in the maximal tetanic force (7.5±0.94 g versus 0.8±0.2 g; p=≤0.000001) elicited by ONS in the engrafted OST group of SOD1G93A mice at late-stage disease, compared to age-matched untrained SOD1G93A mice (132.4±6.8 days versus 133±6.9 days; n=7 and 11, respectively; Figure 5C–G and Appendix 1—table 3), although OST did not alter contractile rate characteristics (Figure 5—figure supplement 5A–C).
evidence: This is supported by isometric muscle tension physiology data shown in Figure 5C-G.

claim: In mice that underwent OST, acute ONS elicits up to 22.7% (±4.5) of total residual muscle force produced by supra-maximal ENS.
source: Moreover, quantitative comparison of the maximum force elicited by ONS compared to ENS of TS muscles in late-stage SOD1G93A mice (Figure 5H), showed that in mice that underwent OST, acute ONS elicits up to 22.7% (±4.5) of total residual muscle force produced by supra-maximal ENS, which activates both endogenous and engrafted motor neurons (Figure 5I), in contrast to only 1.46% (±0.18) in untrained SOD1G93A mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 6A, B).
evidence: This is supported by physiological data shown in Figure 5H and 5I.

claim: OST represents a >13-fold improvement in force generation compared to untrained mice.
source: This represents a remarkable >13-fold improvement in force generation.
evidence: This is calculated from the comparison of ONS-evoked force as a percentage of total muscle capacity between trained and untrained mice.

claim: Repetitive ONS pulses did not induce rapid muscle fatigue, whereas equivalent pulses of ENS stimulation did result in rapid muscle fatigue.
source: Furthermore, as we previously reported in nerve-ligated WT mice, 22 delivery of repetitive ONS pulses (250ms bursts of 20 Hz illumination, every 1 s, for 180 s duration) to induce rhythmic, submaximal contraction of the TS muscle did not induce rapid muscle fatigue, whereas equivalent pulses of ENS stimulation of the contralateral TS muscle did result in rapid muscle fatigue (Figure 5K).
evidence: This is supported by fatigue trace recordings shown in Figure 5K.

claim: The average CSA of muscle fibres innervated by engrafted ChR2+ motor neurons were similar in size to fibres still innervated by residual endogenous motor neurons (922.3 vs 1018.3 μm2; p=≤0.85).
source: The dCALMS analysis revealed that the average CSA of muscle fibres innervated by engrafted ChR2+ motor neurons were similar in size to fibres still innervated by residual endogenous motor neurons (922.3 vs 1018.3 μm2; p=≤0.85; Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by dCALMS analysis data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The CSA of muscle fibres innervated by ChR2+ motor neurons was significantly greater than fibres with completely denervated endplates (average CSA = 525.4 μm2; p=≤0.00001).
source: Importantly, the CSA of muscle fibres innervated by ChR2+ motor neurons was significantly greater than fibres with completely denervated endplates (average CSA = 525.4 μm2; p=≤0.00001) or fibres whose innervation status could not be determined (average CSA = 668.8 μm2; p ≤0.0003), since the endplate was outside the scanned region of interest.
evidence: This is supported by dCALMS analysis data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Replacement stem cell-derived motor neurons can robustly and reliably reinnervate target muscles in the highly aggressive SOD1G93A mouse model of ALS, even when engrafted after onset of overt symptoms.
source: This study shows for the first time that replacement stem cell-derived motor neurons can robustly and reliably reinnervate target muscles in the highly aggressive SOD1G93A mouse model of ALS, even when engrafted after onset of overt symptoms; moreover, the restored innervation can be maintained even until extremely late-stage disease.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data throughout the manuscript showing graft survival and muscle reinnervation.

claim: Regular optical stimulation training (OST) can reinforce connectivity between engrafted motor neurons and muscle fibres.
source: Furthermore, our findings suggest that engrafted ChR2+ motor neurons can not only provide an interface to safely and selectively control the function of targeted muscle but, also, that regular optical stimulation training (OST) can be used to: (i) reinforce connectivity between engrafted motor neurons and muscle fibres; (ii) significantly enhance the maximal force elicited by optical stimulation of the targeted muscle; and (iii) prevent atrophy of muscle fibres that are reinnervated by engrafted motor neurons.
evidence: This is supported by the physiological and histological data comparing trained and untrained mice.

claim: Affected muscles in the highly aggressive SOD1G93A ALS model remain receptive to reinnervation by healthy engrafted motor neurons, even until late-stage disease.
source: Our findings clearly demonstrate that affected muscles, even in the highly aggressive SOD1G93A ALS model, remain receptive to reinnervation by healthy engrafted motor neurons, even until late-stage disease.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data showing successful reinnervation in late-stage disease mice.

claim: Motor neuron subtype identity appears to be redundant for innervating the mixed fibre type TS muscle group in SOD1G93A mice.
source: Since differentiation methods that yield either fast-firing or slow-firing motor neurons did not appear to affect the ability of engrafted motor neurons to innervate the mixed fibre type TS muscle group in SOD1G93A mice, motor neuron subtype identity appears to be redundant in this case.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing no significant difference between motor neuron subtypes.

claim: A single type of motor neuron, produced at scale, could potentially be used to target a large number of different muscles in each patient.
source: Therefore, a single type of motor neuron, produced at scale, could potentially be used to target a large number of different muscles in each patient.
evidence: This is inferred from the finding that motor neuron subtype identity does not affect innervation.

claim: H57-597 mAb treatment was well tolerated during transient administration from symptom-onset up until late-stage disease in SOD1G93A mice.
source: Our data shows that H57-597 mAb treatment was well tolerated during transient administration from symptom-onset up until late-stage disease in SOD1G93A mice, however, the aggressive disease progression in this model precludes investigation of longer-term effects and it remains to be seen how long-term TCR-β-based immunosuppression may be tolerated in ALS patients.
evidence: This is based on observations from the study showing no adverse effects during the treatment period.

claim: Immunosuppression per se is not an impediment to this cell therapy strategy.
source: Therefore, immunosuppression per se, is not an impediment to this strategy.
evidence: This is inferred from clinical trial data showing ALS patients can tolerate immunosuppression.

claim: The use of allogeneic donor cells with a safe and effective immunosuppression regimen means that a future cell therapy could potentially be universally compatible with all ALS patients.
source: The use of allogeneic donor cells, with a safe and effective immunosuppression regimen, means that a future cell therapy could potentially be universally compatible with all ALS patients, which would significantly reduce costs and simplify the regulatory approval process, compared to individually tailored autologous cell grafts.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about future applications based on the current findings.

claim: Immunogenicity of the ChR2 protein could mean that some form of immunosuppression may be necessary for any optogenetic therapy in the peripheral nervous system.
source: The generation of HLA-matched super donor hiPSC lines may further mitigate the need for immunosuppression (Turner et al., 2013), however, immunogenicity of the ChR2 protein could mean that some form of immunosuppression may be necessary for any optogenetic therapy in the peripheral nervous system, including viral delivery (Maimon et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative claim supported by a citation to Maimon et al., 2018.

claim: The anatomical separation of specific nerve branches in humans means that this approach could be used to target and independently control large numbers of muscles in each individual ALS patient.
source: The anatomical separation of specific nerve branches in humans means that this approach could be used to target and independently control large numbers of muscles in each individual ALS patient.
evidence: This is based on anatomical knowledge and inference from the experimental approach.

claim: Existing ENS devices developed to correct foot drop could be readily adapted to assist ambulatory function in early-stage ALS patients.
source: For example, the common peroneal nerve is highly accessible from a neurosurgical perspective and existing ENS devices, developed to correct foot drop for other neurological disorders (Hausmann et al., 2015), could be readily adapted to assist ambulatory function in early-stage ALS patients.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about future applications supported by a citation to Hausmann et al., 2015.

claim: This combinatorial therapeutic strategy is highly compatible with brain computer interface (BCI) technology.
source: This combinatorial therapeutic strategy, comprising allogeneic donor cells, an effective immunosuppression regimen and optical stimulation device, is highly compatible with the rapidly evolving field of brain computer interface (BCI) technology.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about future integration with BCI technology.

claim: BCI could be used to decode a paralyzed patient's intention to perform a given movement in order to control the activity of the engrafted motor neurons.
source: BCI could be used to decode a paralyzed patient's intention to perform a given movement in order to control the activity of the engrafted motor neurons, which provide the necessary interface to execute the intended movement via a wearable optical stimulation device.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about future applications of the technology.

claim: This strategy has broad utility for a wide range of other neurogenic causes of paralysis, such as spinal cord injury and stroke.
source: Moreover, this strategy also has broad utility for a wide range of other neurogenic causes of paralysis, such as spinal cord injury and stroke.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential applications beyond ALS.

claim: ChR2+ motor neurons were derived from a mouse embryonic stem cell (mESC) line using a well-established protocol.
source: ChR2+ motor neurons were derived from our previously characterized mouse embryonic stem cell (mESC) line (Bryson et al., 2014) and differentiated using a well-established protocol (Wichterle et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bryson et al., 2014 and Wichterle et al., 2002.

claim: Donor ChR2+ motor neurons were generated from an mESC line originating from the 129S1/SvImJ mouse strain.
source: Since these donor ChR2+ motor neurons were generated from an mESC line originating from the 129S1/SvImJ mouse strain (Appendix 1—table 1) and recipient mice SOD1G93A mice were on a congenic C57BL/6 J genetic background, they constitute an allogeneic source of donor cells.
evidence: This is based on the genetic background information provided in the manuscript.

claim: Recipient SOD1G93A mice were on a congenic C57BL/6 J genetic background.
source: Since these donor ChR2+ motor neurons were generated from an mESC line originating from the 129S1/SvImJ mouse strain (Appendix 1—table 1) and recipient mice SOD1G93A mice were on a congenic C57BL/6 J genetic background, they constitute an allogeneic source of donor cells.
evidence: This is based on the genetic background information provided in the manuscript.

claim: Allogeneic cells are likely to provide a more cost-effective, off-the-shelf cell therapy platform, compared to generating individual, patient-specific batches of cells suitable for autologous engraftment.
source: Importantly, allogeneic cells are likely to provide a more cost-effective, off-the-shelf cell therapy platform, compared to generating individual, patient-specific batches of cells suitable for autologous engraftment.
evidence: This is based on general knowledge about cell therapy manufacturing and economics.

claim: Engrafted ChR2+ motor neurons were capable of surviving for up to 14 days without immunosuppression.
source: Interestingly, assessment of shorter timepoints revealed that engrafted ChR2+ motor neurons were capable of surviving for up to 14 days (data not shown).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations at shorter timepoints.

claim: If engrafted motor neurons can evade the host immune response, they can functionally reinnervate target muscles for a therapeutically relevant timescale in the highly aggressive SOD1G93A model of ALS.
source: These findings suggest that if the engrafted motor neurons can evade the host immune response, they can functionally reinnervate target muscles for a therapeutically relevant timescale in this highly aggressive model of ALS.
evidence: This is inferred from the rare cases of graft survival and functional reinnervation observed without immunosuppression.

claim: FK506 has been reported to promote axon regeneration after nerve injury in rats.
source: In an effort to enhance graft survival, we first tested the calcineurin inhibitor (CNI), tacrolimus (FK506), which is not only routinely used to facilitate solid organ allograft survival in humans but has also been reported to promote axon regeneration after nerve injury in rats (Gold et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gold et al., 1995.

claim: Peripheral neuropathy is a known adverse event associated with calcineurin inhibitors.
source: Since peripheral neuropathy is a known adverse event associated with calcineurin inhibitors (Arnold et al., 2013), it is possible that FK506 treatment alone may adversely affect endogenous or engrafted motor axons.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Arnold et al., 2013.

claim: The complete protection of engrafted ChR2+ motor neurons by FK506 confirmed that host-vs-graft rejection was responsible for the poor long-term graft survival observed in the absence of immunosuppression.
source: Importantly, however, the complete protection of engrafted ChR2+ motor neurons by FK506 did confirm that host-vs-graft rejection was responsible for the poor long-term graft survival observed in the absence of immunosuppression, rather than disease related neurotoxicity.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that FK506 enabled complete graft survival.

claim: OST did not alter contractile rate characteristics.
source: In confirmation of our hypothesis, there was a highly significant, 9.4-fold, increase in the maximal tetanic force (7.5±0.94 g versus 0.8±0.2 g; p=≤0.000001) elicited by ONS in the engrafted OST group of SOD1G93A mice at late-stage disease, compared to age-matched untrained SOD1G93A mice (132.4±6.8 days versus 133±6.9 days; n=7 and 11, respectively; Figure 5C–G and Appendix 1—table 3), although OST did not alter contractile rate characteristics (Figure 5—figure supplement 5A–C).
evidence: This is supported by physiological data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5A–C.

claim: In engrafted SOD1G93A mice that did not undergo OST, the extremely weak twitch contractions in response to ONS precluded interrogation of individual motor unit force values and determination of motor units number estimates (MUNE) in most mice.
source: In engrafted SOD1G93A mice that did not undergo OST, the extremely weak twitch contractions in response to ONS precluded interrogation of individual motor unit force values and determination of motor units number estimates (MUNE) in most mice.
evidence: This is based on the physiological analysis of untrained mice.

claim: In SOD1G93A mice that underwent OST, the significantly increased contractile response to ONS enabled clear separation of individual motor unit values.
source: In contrast, in SOD1G93A mice that underwent OST, the significantly increased contractile response to ONS enabled clear separation of individual motor unit values (Figure 5J), enabling MUNE values to be determined (Figure 5—figure supplement 5D).
evidence: This is supported by physiological data shown in Figure 5J and Figure 5—figure supplement 5D.

claim: High-resolution 3D imaging of the entire muscle to determine muscle fibre innervation status and fibre diameter information is not feasible.
source: Since NMJs comprise an extremely small volume of the entire muscle, high-resolution 3D imaging of the entire muscle to determine muscle fibre innervation status and fibre diameter information is not feasible.
evidence: This is based on technical limitations of imaging methods.

claim: A novel technique termed digital Cross-sectional area Analysis from Longitudinal Muscle Sections (dCALMS) was developed to assess muscle fiber innervation status and fiber diameter.
source: Therefore, we developed a novel technique, termed digital Cross-sectional area Analysis from Longitudinal Muscle Sections (dCALMS), in order to assess these properties.
evidence: This is a methodological development described in the manuscript.

claim: The CSA of muscle fibres innervated by ChR2+ motor neurons was significantly greater than fibres whose innervation status could not be determined (average CSA = 668.8 μm2; p ≤0.0003).
source: Importantly, the CSA of muscle fibres innervated by ChR2+ motor neurons was significantly greater than fibres with completely denervated endplates (average CSA = 525.4 μm2; p=≤0.00001) or fibres whose innervation status could not be determined (average CSA = 668.8 μm2; p ≤0.0003), since the endplate was outside the scanned region of interest.
evidence: This is supported by dCALMS analysis data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The highly significant improvements in muscle innervation, atrophy prevention and maximum contractile force as a result of daily OST confirms that stimulation-induced activity is necessary to maximize connectivity between engrafted motor neurons and their target muscles.
source: The highly significant improvements in muscle innervation, atrophy prevention and maximum contractile force, as a result of the daily OST regimen, confirms that stimulation-induced activity is necessary to maximize connectivity between engrafted motor neurons and their target muscles.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of trained and untrained mice.

claim: The prevailing view in the ALS field is that spinal motor neuron pathology first manifests at the nerve terminal.
source: The prevailing view in the ALS field is that spinal motor neuron pathology first manifests at the nerve terminal and that muscle fibres are likely to actively contribute to degeneration of endogenous motor neurons in ALS (Scaricamazza et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Scaricamazza et al., 2021.

claim: Muscle fibres are likely to actively contribute to degeneration of endogenous motor neurons in ALS.
source: The prevailing view in the ALS field is that spinal motor neuron pathology first manifests at the nerve terminal and that muscle fibres are likely to actively contribute to degeneration of endogenous motor neurons in ALS (Scaricamazza et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Scaricamazza et al., 2021.

claim: Skeletal muscles have complex functions in overall metabolic homeostasis, thermoregulation, venous return and maintenance of blood volume.
source: Since skeletal muscles are not simply biomechanical actuators, but have complex functions in overall metabolic homeostasis, thermoregulation, venous return and maintenance of blood volume, the ability to prevent muscle atrophy using OST, is likely, by itself, to have major health benefits for ALS patients.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about muscle physiology.

claim: The use of electrical nerve stimulation (ENS) to control muscle function is likely to accelerate degeneration of remaining motor axon terminals.
source: In contrast, the use of electrical nerve stimulation (ENS) to control muscle function or, indeed, ENS-based exercise programs is likely to accelerate degeneration of remaining motor axon terminals (Guimarães-Costa et al., 2019), and is therefore unlikely to be safe.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Guimarães-Costa et al., 2019.

claim: The highly selective nature of ONS does not activate or interfere with endogenous motor neuron function.
source: Unlike ENS, the highly selective nature of ONS does not activate or interfere with endogenous motor neuron function and due to its ability to recruit motor units in physiological order, ONS has the added significant benefit of avoiding rapid muscle fatigue (Llewellyn et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on the properties of optogenetic stimulation and supported by a citation to Llewellyn et al., 2010.

claim: The ability to combat muscle atrophy using OST could extend the ability of targeted muscles to execute functionally useful movements, potentially indefinitely in ALS patients.
source: The ability to combat muscle atrophy, using OST, could extend the ability of targeted to execute functionally useful movements, potentially indefinitely in ALS patients.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about future therapeutic potential.

claim: Existing T-cell targeting monoclonal antibodies, such as OKT-3, have been clinically approved.
source: Existing T-cell targeting monoclonal antibodies, such as OKT-3, have been clinically approved (Page et al., 2013) and, importantly, this form of immunosuppression overcomes severe adverse effects that we observed with the commonly used CNI-based immunosuppressant, tacrolimus (FK506).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Page et al., 2013.

claim: A similar immunosuppression regimen involving a CD25 (IL2) targeting monoclonal antibody, Basiliximab, along with glucocorticoid and tacrolimus maintenance therapy, has been shown to be safe but poorly tolerated in ALS patients.
source: A similar immunosuppression regimen involving a CD25 (IL2) targeting monoclonal antibody, Basiliximab, along with glucocorticoid and tacrolimus maintenance therapy, has been shown to be safe but poorly tolerated in ALS patients, as an independent investigative approach (Fournier et al., 2018), as well as part of a separate clinical trial assessing intraspinal grafts of neural precursor cells in ALS patients (Mazzini et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fournier et al., 2018 and Mazzini et al., 2019.

claim: The generation of HLA-matched super donor hiPSC lines may further mitigate the need for immunosuppression.
source: The generation of HLA-matched super donor hiPSC lines may further mitigate the need for immunosuppression (Turner et al., 2013), however, immunogenicity of the ChR2 protein could mean that some form of immunosuppression may be necessary for any optogenetic therapy in the peripheral nervous system, including viral delivery (Maimon et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Turner et al., 2013.

claim: The common peroneal nerve is highly accessible from a neurosurgical perspective.
source: For example, the common peroneal nerve is highly accessible from a neurosurgical perspective and existing ENS devices, developed to correct foot drop for other neurological disorders (Hausmann et al., 2015), could be readily adapted to assist ambulatory function in early-stage ALS patients.
evidence: This is based on anatomical knowledge.

claim: Existing multichannel ENS devices have been developed to control more complex ADLs in high-level spinal cord injury (SCI) patients.
source: In the longer term, existing multichannel ENS devices, which have been developed to control more complex ADLs in high-level spinal cord injury (SCI) patients (Memberg et al., 2014), could also be adapted into a minimally invasive, transcutaneous optical stimulation device (Maimon et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Memberg et al., 2014 and Maimon et al., 2017.

claim: This novel approach would entirely bypass the severe damage that occurs throughout the entire CNS in ALS patients and enable autologous control of movement.
source: This novel approach would entirely bypass the severe damage that occurs throughout the entire CNS in ALS patients and enable autologous control of movement.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about future therapeutic potential.

claim: Further investigation is required to confirm that the strategy can be applied to alternate models of ALS with a longer lifespan.
source: Although the findings of this study clearly demonstrate that our combinatorial cell therapy approach is effective in a highly aggressive mouse model of ALS, further investigation is required in order to confirm that the strategy can be applied to alternate model of ALS, with a longer lifespan, in order to fully explore the long-term efficacy of the approach, particularly in terms of chronic allograft survival using a transient immunosuppression approach.
evidence: This acknowledges limitations of the current study and future research needs.

claim: It is possible that some form of maintenance therapy may be required to confer long term graft survival.
source: It is possible that some form of maintenance therapy may also be required to confer long term graft survival.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential future requirements.

claim: The biggest challenge will be to demonstrate that human optogenetically-modified motor neurons, derived from either induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) or human ESCs, are capable of reinnervating target muscles in the same manner as mESC-derived motor neurons.
source: Of course, the biggest challenge will be to demonstrate that human optogenetically-modified motor neurons, derived from either induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) or human ESCs, are capable of reinnervating target muscles in the same manner as we have demonstrated for mESC-derived motor neurons.
evidence: This acknowledges a key challenge for clinical translation.

claim: It will be necessary to scale this cell therapy strategy up, using larger animal models that more accurately recapitulate human-scale anatomy.
source: It will also be necessary to scale this cell therapy strategy up, using larger animal models that more accurately recapitulate human-scale anatomy.
evidence: This acknowledges a requirement for future preclinical development.

claim: The findings of this study provide strong support for this novel cell therapy, which, if successful, could finally begin to deliver major health benefits for ALS patients.
source: Despite these remaining challenges, the findings of this study provide strong support for this novel cell therapy, which, if successful, could finally begin to deliver major health benefits for ALS patients.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the potential impact of the research.
